name: Anarlog
tagline: An AI notepad for meetings, with desktop, mobile, and developer interfaces.
hook: Separate TypeScript and Rust guides to component checks, native release evidence, generated files, and database constraints.
summary: Anarlog gives each TypeScript and Rust component its own checks. It separates desktop JavaScript tests from scheduled native jobs, requires evidence from the exact release candidate, and names generated files and database constraints. Simple CLI screens are told not to adopt reducer and effect machinery they do not need.

techniques.title: Match checks to the affected component
techniques.body: The verification table covers desktop, web, API, CLI, mobile, databases, billing, and a separate enterprise workspace. It warns that workflow path filters can miss consumers of shared packages.
techniques.quote: A skipped workflow/job is not passing coverage.

techniques.title: Verify the job and the candidate
techniques.body: Native desktop and mobile coverage is not implied by a green PR result. Release verification requires the relevant job on the recorded candidate SHA.
techniques.quote: Check each required job and SHA, not only the aggregate green result.

techniques.title: Name generated outputs and their owners
techniques.body: OpenAPI, native bindings, permissions, and translations each have an owning generation command. Stable regeneration is required; hand-editing output would leave the source of truth unchanged.
techniques.quote: Regenerate native bindings and permissions using their owning Rust build/generator; do not hand-edit generated output.

techniques.title: Design migrations for the installed older build
techniques.body: Nightly and stable share a database. The file requires additive migrations by default and an explicit marker when older versions must refuse to open a newer schema.
techniques.quote: Nightly and stable desktop builds share one database, so a breaking migration published in Nightly locks stable out until stable ships it.

techniques.title: Scale command architecture to its state
techniques.body: The reducer/effect/runtime split is conditional on actual orchestration or state complexity. Simple browse and select flows are directed to a smaller structure.
techniques.quote: Use the full reducer/effect/runtime split only when the command has async orchestration, a multi-step workflow, or substantial state transitions that benefit from reducer-style tests.

steal: Map changed components to complete validation jobs, including setup.
Report skipped checks separately from passing checks.
Bind release evidence to one immutable candidate.
Name generated files together with the command that owns them.
Document how schema changes affect older installed clients.
